prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Maker-of-sevens in the scheme of things From earth to star; Thy cycle holds whatever is fate, and Over the border the bar. Though rank and fierce the mariner Sailing the seven seas, He prays, as he holds his glass to his eyes, Coaxing the Pleiades. I cannot love them; and I feel your glad Chiding from the grave, That my all was only worth at all, what Joy to you it gave. These seven links the Law compelled For the human chain— I cannot love them; and you, oh, Seven-fold months in Flanders slain! A jungle there, a cave here, bred six And a million years, Sure and strong, mate for mate, such Love as culture fears; I gave you clear the oil and wine; You saved me your hob and hearth— See how even life may be ere the Sickle comes and leaves a swath. But I can wait the seven of moons, Or years I spare, Hoarding the heart’s plenty, nor spend A drop, nor share— So long but outlives a smile and A silken gown; Then gaily I reach up from my shroud, And you, glory-clad, reach down.

Maker-of-sevens in the scheme of things,

outputs.L2:
Shaper of sevens within the order of all things,  
From the ground below to the stars above,  
Your turning circle contains all that destiny allows,  
And at the boundary stands the barrier.

Although the sailor is rough, proud, and fierce,  
Voyaging across the seven seas,  
He lifts his glass to his eye and offers a prayer,  
Trying to draw the Pleiades nearer.

I cannot bring myself to love them;  
And I sense your happy rebuke from the grave:  
That everything I possessed had value only  
In the happiness it brought to you.

The Law required these seven bonds  
To make the chain of humankind—  
I cannot love them; and you, ah,  
Seven-months-fold, killed in Flanders!

One was formed in a jungle, another in a cave,  
Across six million years,  
Certain and powerful, mate joined to mate,  
With a love that civilization is afraid of.

I gave you the pure oil and wine;  
You kept for me your fireside and home—  
Look how complete even life can be  
Before the Sickle arrives and cuts its path.

Yet I am able to wait through seven moons,  
Or through whatever years I have left,  
Storing the heart’s abundance, spending none,  
Not sharing even a single drop—

So long as a smile survives a little longer,  
And a gown of silk remains;  
Then, joyfully, I lift my hands from my burial cloth,  
And you, dressed in glory, bend down to me.
outputs.L3:
The poem centers on the recurring symbol of seven, using it as a force that links fate, time, love, and human experience. Rather than functioning as a simple number, seven becomes a pattern through which the speaker understands the world. It suggests order, repetition, and mystery, connecting personal grief to larger cycles that seem to govern both human life and the universe.

The speaker reflects on sailors, stars, and the Pleiades in order to connect earthly struggle with cosmic patterns. Sailors depend on the stars for direction, especially when facing danger and uncertainty at sea. By invoking the Pleiades, a constellation traditionally associated with navigation, myth, and seasonal change, the poem places human suffering within a vast celestial framework. The speaker’s private sorrow is therefore not isolated; it becomes part of a broader universe shaped by recurring signs and ancient patterns.

At the heart of the poem is mourning for a lost beloved. The speaker feels the absence of this person so deeply that even things once valued have lost their meaning. What mattered before mattered largely because it brought joy to the beloved. Without that person, the world appears diminished, and the speaker can no longer love certain places, objects, or experiences in the same way. This grief reveals how love can transform perception: the beloved gave significance to the world, and their loss drains that world of its former brightness.

The poem also contrasts primal, enduring love with the destructive forces of time, death, and war. Love is presented as something ancient and elemental, stronger than ordinary attachments and rooted deeply in human nature. Yet it exists in a world marked by decay, violence, and separation. Time erodes, death divides, and war destroys, but the speaker’s love resists these forces. Even though the beloved is gone, the emotional bond remains powerful, suggesting that love may outlast the conditions that threaten it.

Finally, the speaker expresses a willingness to wait beyond months, years, and even death for reunion with the beloved. This patience is not passive but deeply devoted. The speaker imagines love extending beyond earthly limits, refusing to be ended by time or mortality. In this way, the poem becomes both an elegy and a declaration of faith: although separation defines the present, the speaker continues to hope for a reunion that transcends the boundaries of human life.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents a meditation on grief, love, fate, and recurrence, drawing its emotional power from the repeated symbolic motif of “seven.” This number suggests completion, destiny, and spiritual significance, giving the poem a sense that personal sorrow is not isolated or accidental but part of a larger pattern. Through cosmic imagery, the speaker places private loss against the vastness of stars, time, and the universe, suggesting that grief reaches beyond ordinary human experience. Maritime images of waves, tides, ships, or distant shores evoke separation, danger, and the uncertain journey between life and death. Biblical echoes deepen the poem’s spiritual dimension, connecting suffering to faith, sacrifice, and the possibility of redemption. Wartime imagery, meanwhile, frames loss as violent, historical, and collective, showing how private mourning can be shaped by forces larger than the individual.

At the center of the poem is the tension between death’s finality and love’s endurance. The speaker recognizes the pain of absence, yet refuses to accept that death has completely destroyed the bond between the living and the dead. Memory becomes a form of resistance: by recalling moments of happiness, tenderness, and shared life, the speaker preserves what has been lost. These remembered joys do not erase suffering, but they give it meaning. Grief becomes more than emptiness; it becomes proof of love’s depth and continuing power.

The recurring pattern suggested by the “seven” motif also implies that separation may not be the end of the story. The poem imagines time as cyclical rather than merely linear, allowing for return, renewal, and reunion. In this way, the beloved remains present through memory, symbol, and hope. The poem ultimately transforms mourning into a vision of continuity: love survives beyond death, joy illuminates sorrow, and the pain of parting is reshaped by the belief that what has been deeply loved is never wholly lost.
outputs.L5:
**Maker, From, Thy**

From the quiet places of the heart, a voice rises in gratitude to the Maker of all things. Every dawn, every breath, and every moment of hope feels like a gift shaped by unseen hands. The world, with its light and shadow, reminds us that life is not merely something we possess, but something entrusted to us.

O Maker, from Thy wisdom comes the strength to endure, the courage to begin again, and the grace to see beauty even in difficult days. Thy presence can be found in the smallest acts of kindness, in the patience of love, and in the peace that follows faith.

From Thy creation, we learn humility. From Thy mercy, we learn compassion. From Thy guidance, we learn the path toward goodness. And through every season, the soul remembers: it is never truly alone when it turns back to its Maker.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a cryptic modernist poem with archaic diction that weaves together the number seven, the Pleiades, fate, sailors, grief, Flanders, and love beyond death.
counterfactuals.output:
**Heptad for the Drowned**

Seven were the lamps i’ the bitter heaven,  
seven—yet one went veiled in rain;  
the Pleiades, like widows’ pins,  
pricked night above the Flemish plain.

Lo, fate, that blindfold sempstress, sewed  
our names in salt and scarlet thread;  
the sailors heard her shuttle knock  
beneath the keel, among the dead.

At Ypres, love wore mud for gold,  
and poppies spake in tongues of rust;  
“O heart,” quoth grief, “be thou not whole—  
what’s whole is soonest turned to dust.”

Yet thou, beyond the worm’s black tithe,  
beyond the bell, the trench, the foam,  
didst lift thy face through seven stars  
and call the foundered mariners home.

So still I count—one, two, the lost—  
till number break and skies unseam;  
and in the seventh wound of night,  
thy mouth returns, a burning dream.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a poem in the style of early 20th-century war elegy, full of symbolic references to sevens, stars, graves, and a beloved reaching down from heaven.
counterfactuals.output:
At dusk the seventh bugle failed and fell,  
A silver star drowned in the guns’ red breath;  
And seven fields lay silent under shell,  
Each furrow sown with the black seed of death.  

We counted seven names upon the stone,  
And seven lamps along the trench were gone;  
The moon stood pale as bone on bone,  
Keeping her watch till the bitter dawn.  

O love, above the shattered weather,  
Above the smoke where the lost stars lean,  
Did you not stoop through heaven’s heather  
With hands as soft as they had been?  

I felt you reach where the clay was clinging,  
Down through the dark with a tender flame;  
The larks were broken, but still were singing  
Somewhere beyond the roll-call of my name.  

Seven stars burned over the crowded graves,  
Seven tears shone on the wire’s cold thorn;  
And all night long, like mourning waves,  
The dead men waited to be born.  

Then you, my dear, from the height of morning,  
Bent through the blue with a rose-white hand;  
And touched the earth without a warning,  
And called me home from the foreign land.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dense, fragmented lyric poem about mourning a lover killed in Flanders, including images of the seven seas, seven moons, the Sickle, oil and wine, and a shroud.
counterfactuals.output:
Flanders —  
mud-mouth, poppy-throat,  
your name goes under.

I count the seven seas  
on one torn glove;  
salt, salt, salt, salt, salt, salt, salt —  
none return you.

Above me: seven moons,  
all bruised coin, all bone-lantern,  
all watching the Sickle  
lean down through the wheat  
where your breath was cut.

Oil for the wound.  
Wine for the ground.  
I pour both out —  
black shine, red shine —  
and the field drinks  
like a widow.

Your letters smell of rain,  
iron, horse-sweat, smoke;  
each word a little shroud  
I fold and fold  
until my hands vanish.

Beloved,  
in Flanders the dead lie close,  
root to rib, seed to socket,  
and spring comes cruel  
with its green absolutions.

I have no country now  
but your absence:  
a trench, a torn sleeve,  
a cup of oil,  
a cup of wine,  
the seven seas inside my chest,  
the seven moons nailed over them,

and the Sickle —  
bright, patient —  
reaping even my sleep.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an imitation of a mystical Victorian/Georgian poem where the speaker rejects “seven” earthly things but waits faithfully for reunion with the dead beloved.
counterfactuals.output:
**Seven Things**

I would not have the rose, my dear,  
Though red it leans against the pane;  
Its heart is only summer’s fire,  
And summer dies in rain.  

I would not have the golden cup,  
Though kings have kissed its shining rim;  
What wine could warm this widowed mouth,  
That drank farewell from him?  

I would not have the harp at eve,  
Though all its trembling silver sings;  
One footfall on the stair were more  
Than all its wounded strings.  

I would not have the laurel crown,  
Though Fame should bind it on my hair;  
The dust that lies upon his grave  
Is greener, dearer there.  

I would not have the bridal veil,  
Though white as moonlight it might be;  
My troth was given beneath the yew,  
And death has married me.  

I would not have the lamp of gold,  
Though saints might tend its starry flame;  
I keep one candle in my heart,  
And feed it with his name.  

I would not have the world itself—  
Its gardens, bells, and morning skies;  
For earth is but a foreign inn  
Since he has closed his eyes.  

Yet I will wait where shadows bloom,  
And count the church-clock’s ghostly chime,  
Till God shall lift the blackthorn bough  
That bars the door of time.  

Then through the dusk, with quiet face,  
He shall return, no longer pale;  
And I shall know his hand in mine  
Beyond the mortal veil.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an obscure, old-fashioned free-verse elegy using repeated references to seven, cosmic order, mariners, the Pleiades, human evolution, and resurrection-like reunion.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Seventh Watch**

O thou that wentest down by the black quay  
when the lamps were few,  
and the tide, like an old judge,  
muttered its statutes under weed and moon—  
I name thee not,  
for names are nets,  
and the dead go through them shining.

Seven were the bells that found thee.  
Seven the gulls that veered and vanished.  
Seven the cold stars over the mast,  
set in their antique order,  
as if some hidden hand,  
older than priestcraft, older than flint,  
had ranged the heavens for thy passage.

The mariners stood dumb,  
their faces salt and scripture,  
and one, who had rounded Thule in his youth,  
whispered of the Pleiades—  
those little burning sisters  
lost and found in the black field—  
and would not weep.

O Pleiades, small choir of the upper deep,  
ye that have watched the ape rise upright,  
the hand learn fire,  
the skull grow troubled with eternity,  
the clay become a questioner of stars—  
did ye behold my beloved pass  
beyond the seventh door?

For there is order, they say,  
cosmic and severe:  
wheel within wheel,  
sphere answering sphere,  
dust returning by appointed roads,  
the comets keeping their ragged vows.  
Yet what decree accounts for longing?  
What algebra restores the voice  
that once called bread by its homely name?

I have sat among fossils and prayer-books.  
I have heard the bone confess its lineage—  
fin, paw, hand,  
and the hand at last laid gently on another hand.  
From ooze to eye,  
from fang to psalm,  
from hunger to the kiss farewell,  
we have climbed, not knowing,  
toward the grief of being human.

Seven nights I kept the window wide.  
Seven dawns came grey as ashes.  
The mariners’ wives passed below,  
bearing linen, onions, and rumor;  
the sea kept its counsel.  
Only the Pleiades, faint in the paling west,  
seemed like a cluster of remembered faces  
half-risen through sleep.

And if there be a farther harbor,  
not charted on vellum nor sung in the taverns,  
where the drowned and the dust-worn meet,  
where the sundered are gathered  
as sparks to one fire,  
then wait for me there  
by the seventh lamp.

For I too shall put off this garment of weather,  
this evolved sorrow,  
this body taught by ages to stand upright  
only to bow at graves.  
I too shall descend,  
and in that deep re-ordering  
of marrow, star, and breath,  
perhaps thy hand will find mine again.

Then shall the mariners sing without salt in their throats.  
Then shall the Pleiades be no more distant  
than candles set upon a supper-board.  
Then shall seven become one,  
and one become all,  
and the old cosmic law,  
so sternly written in darkness,  
be read at last as mercy.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
